lessons.title: Grinding and Surface Preparation
lessons.body: Before you paint or coat steel, you must prepare the surface. Dirt, rust, mill scale, and oil will make any finish fail. Start by inspecting the steel. Look for rust (red or brown), mill scale (dark grey flaky layer), weld spatter, and sharp edges. Use a wire brush or scraper to remove loose rust and dirt. For heavier rust, use a chipping hammer. Then, use an angle grinder with a grinding wheel (typically 115mm or 230mm diameter) to grind down welds, smooth edges, and remove mill scale. Hold the grinder at a 15-30 degree angle and move it steadily. Don't press too hard; let the tool do the work. For corners and tight spots, use a die grinder or a file. After grinding, switch to a sanding disc (40-80 grit) to smooth the surface. Finally, clean the surface with a solvent like acetone or methylated spirits to remove oil and dust. In Africa, where humidity and heat can be high, work in the shade and avoid leaving bare steel overnight. A properly prepared surface should look uniformly grey or white metal, with no shiny spots (which indicate oil) and no dark patches (rust). This step takes time but ensures your coating lasts for years.

lessons.title: Shot Blasting and Sandblasting
lessons.body: Shot blasting and sandblasting are methods to clean steel by firing abrasive particles at high speed. Sandblasting uses silica sand, while shot blasting uses steel shot or grit. Both remove rust, mill scale, and old paint, leaving a rough profile that helps coatings stick. In Africa, sandblasting is common but dangerous: silica dust causes silicosis. Always wear a respirator, goggles, and heavy gloves. Work outdoors or in a well-ventilated area. For small jobs, a portable sandblaster (like a pressure pot) works with a compressor delivering at least 100 PSI. Hold the nozzle 300-500mm from the surface and move in steady passes. For large structures, use a shot blasting machine with a closed cabinet or a centrifugal wheel system. After blasting, the steel should be a uniform grey-white. Blast to SA 2.5 or SA 3 standard (near-white or white metal). Immediately apply a primer within 4 hours to prevent flash rust, especially in humid coastal areas like Mombasa or Lagos. If you don't have equipment, you can hire a mobile blasting service. Remember: never use sand from a river or beach without testing for salt; salt causes rust. Use clean, dry abrasive. Safety first: no blasting near people or animals.

lessons.title: Painting and Coating Systems
lessons.body: Painting steel is not just about colour; it's about protection. A good coating system has three parts: primer, intermediate coat, and topcoat. Primer sticks to the steel and prevents rust. Use a zinc-rich primer for harsh environments, or an epoxy primer for general use. Apply by brush, roller, or spray. For brush, use a 50mm or 75mm natural bristle brush. For spray, use a conventional or airless sprayer. Mix paint thoroughly and thin only as recommended. Apply the primer at 75-100 microns dry film thickness (DFT). Let it dry (usually 4-6 hours at 25Â°C). Then apply an intermediate coat, often epoxy or polyurethane, at 100-150 microns DFT. Finally, the topcoat (polyurethane or enamel) gives colour and UV resistance, at 50-75 microns DFT. Total DFT should be 200-300 microns. In Africa, use paints that resist heat and humidity. Avoid painting in direct sun or when humidity is above 85%. Check with a wet film gauge and dry film gauge. Clean tools with thinner. Store paint away from heat. If you see runs, sags, or brush marks, sand and recoat. A good paint job lasts 5-10 years.

lessons.title: Galvanizing and Metalizing
lessons.body: Galvanizing coats steel with zinc to prevent rust. There are two main types: hot-dip galvanizing and metalizing (also called zinc spraying). Hot-dip galvanizing involves dipping prepared steel into molten zinc at about 450Â°C. The zinc reacts with the steel to form a tough alloy layer. This is done in a factory, so you must send your steel to a galvanizing plant. The coating is typically 50-100 microns thick and lasts 20-50 years, even in coastal areas. For large structures like transmission towers or boat trailers, hot-dip is best. Metalizing, on the other hand, can be done on-site. You use a wire arc or flame spray gun to melt zinc wire and spray it onto the steel. The surface must be blasted to SA 2.5 first. The zinc coating is 100-200 microns thick, but it's porous, so you must seal it with a thin coat of epoxy or polyurethane. Metalizing is good for repairs or for very large objects that can't be dipped. In Africa, hot-dip galvanizing plants are in major cities like Johannesburg, Nairobi, and Lagos. Metalizing equipment is portable but expensive. Both methods require safety gear: respirator, gloves, and face shield. Never weld galvanized steel without removing the zinc first; the fumes are toxic.

lessons.title: Powder Coating
lessons.body: Powder coating is a dry finishing process. Instead of liquid paint, you spray electrostatically charged powder onto a grounded metal part. The powder sticks, then you bake it in an oven at 180-200Â°C for 10-20 minutes. The powder melts and forms a smooth, hard film. Powder coating is tougher than wet paint and comes in many colours. It's great for furniture, fencing, and automotive parts. To powder coat, first clean and pretreat the steel. Blast or phosphate the surface. Then hang the part on a conveyor or rack. Use a powder spray gun (electrostatic) to apply the powder. Aim for 60-100 microns thickness. Too thin and you'll see bare spots; too thick and it may orange-peel. After spraying, cure in an oven. In Africa, powder coating is common in cities like Cairo, Durban, and Accra. Small shops use batch ovens; large factories use conveyor lines. If you don't have an oven, you can't powder coat properly. Some try to use a heat gun, but results are poor. Safety: wear a dust mask and avoid breathing powder. Keep the area clean; powder is flammable. Powder coating is not good for parts that will be welded later; the coating will burn. Also, it's hard to touch up; you need to re-coat the whole part.

lessons.title: Quality Inspection of Finishes
lessons.body: After finishing, you must inspect the coating to ensure it will protect the steel. Start with a visual check. Look for runs, sags, drips, brush marks, holidays (missed spots), and foreign particles. The colour should be uniform. For thickness, use a dry film thickness (DFT) gauge. Take 5-10 readings per square meter. The average should meet the spec, and no single reading should be less than 80% of the spec. For example, if spec is 200 microns, no reading below 160 microns. For adhesion, use a cross-hatch or pull-off test. Cross-hatch: cut a grid with a knife, apply tape, and pull. If paint comes off, adhesion is poor. Pull-off: glue a dolly, pull with a gauge, and note the force. For galvanizing, check thickness with a magnetic gauge and look for bare spots. For powder coating, check for orange peel, pinholes, and colour match. Also check for cure: wipe with MEK (methyl ethyl ketone) â if the coating softens, it's undercured. Document all results. In Africa, humidity and heat can affect curing, so test often. If a coating fails, you must remove it and redo. Quality inspection saves money in the long run.

quiz.q: What is the first step in surface preparation before painting steel?
options: B) Remove dirt, rust, and oil
quiz.explanation: Cleaning removes contaminants that would prevent paint adhesion.

quiz.q: Which tool is best for removing mill scale and smoothing welds?
quiz.explanation: An angle grinder with a grinding wheel is effective for heavy material removal.

quiz.q: What should you use to remove oil and dust after grinding?
quiz.explanation: Solvents dissolve oils and evaporate quickly, leaving a clean surface.

quiz.q: What is a danger of sandblasting with silica sand?
quiz.explanation: Inhaling silica dust causes silicosis, a serious lung disease.

quiz.q: After sandblasting, how soon should you apply primer?
quiz.explanation: Bare steel rusts quickly, especially in humid conditions, so primer must be applied promptly.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a primer in a coating system?
options: B) Stick to steel and prevent rust
quiz.explanation: Primer promotes adhesion and provides corrosion protection.

quiz.q: What is a typical dry film thickness (DFT) for a primer?
quiz.explanation: Primers are usually applied at 75-100 microns DFT.

quiz.q: Which condition should you avoid when painting?
quiz.explanation: High humidity can prevent proper drying and adhesion.

quiz.q: What is hot-dip galvanizing?
options: B) Dipping steel in molten zinc
quiz.explanation: Hot-dip galvanizing involves immersing steel in molten zinc to form a protective alloy layer.

quiz.q: What is metalizing?
quiz.explanation: Metalizing (zinc spraying) uses a spray gun to deposit molten zinc on the surface.

quiz.q: Why must metalized coatings be sealed?
quiz.explanation: Metalized zinc is porous, so a sealer prevents moisture from reaching the steel.

quiz.q: What is a safety concern when welding galvanized steel?
quiz.explanation: Welding galvanized steel releases zinc oxide fumes, which can cause metal fume fever.

quiz.q: What is powder coating?
options: B) Dry powder sprayed and baked
quiz.explanation: Powder coating uses electrostatically charged powder that is baked to form a film.

quiz.q: What temperature is used to cure powder coating?
quiz.explanation: Powder coating typically cures at 180-200Â°C.

quiz.q: What is a common defect in powder coating if too thick?
quiz.explanation: Excessive thickness can cause orange peel texture.

quiz.q: What is the first step in quality inspection of a coating?
quiz.explanation: Visual inspection identifies obvious defects before testing.

quiz.q: What instrument measures dry film thickness?
quiz.explanation: A DFT gauge uses magnetic or eddy current principles to measure coating thickness.

quiz.q: In a cross-hatch adhesion test, what indicates poor adhesion?
quiz.explanation: If paint comes off with the tape, adhesion is insufficient.

quiz.q: What does MEK wipe test check?
quiz.explanation: MEK softens undercured coatings, indicating improper curing.

quiz.q: What is a holiday in coating inspection?
quiz.explanation: A holiday is an area where the coating is missing or too thin.

quiz.q: Which abrasive is safer than silica sand for blasting?
quiz.explanation: Steel grit does not contain silica and can be reused.

quiz.q: What is the typical thickness of a hot-dip galvanized coating?
quiz.explanation: Hot-dip galvanizing typically produces 50-100 microns of zinc.

quiz.q: Which coating system is best for a coastal environment?
quiz.explanation: A three-coat system with zinc-rich primer provides excellent corrosion resistance.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a topcoat?
quiz.explanation: Topcoat provides aesthetics and protects against UV degradation.

quiz.q: How many DFT readings should you take per square meter?
quiz.explanation: Multiple readings ensure the coating is uniformly applied.

quiz.q: What is the minimum acceptable DFT if spec is 200 microns?
quiz.explanation: No single reading should be less than 80% of the specified thickness.

quiz.q: Which method can be done on-site for large structures?
quiz.explanation: Metalizing equipment is portable and can be used in the field.

quiz.q: Why is surface profile important for coating adhesion?
quiz.explanation: A rough profile increases surface area and allows coating to anchor.

quiz.q: What should you do if you find a run in a painted surface?
quiz.explanation: Sanding smooths the run, and recoating restores appearance and protection.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a step in powder coating?
quiz.explanation: Dipping in molten zinc is hot-dip galvanizing, not powder coating.
